Wednesday 9/16/2026 a.m.
Markets edge higher as investors wait for the Fed –
U.S. equity markets rebounded cautiously on Wednesday's open, with bonds rallying too. The S&P 500 index is up 0.2%, led by strong performance among financial and energy names, and mirroring the upbeat tone in European and Asian equity markets overnight. U.S. government bonds, which have sold off sharply in recent weeks on the back of concerns over inflation, higher short-term interest rates, and debt levels, are rallying slightly this morning. This has helped push the closely followed 10-year Treasury yield back below the 5% mark, although at 4.97% this remains near 20-year highs. Oil prices are a little softer today, with WTI crude tracking $104 per barrel, down from $106 yesterday in what remains a headline-driven market.
Retail sales continue to point to resilient consumers –
U.S. retail sales rebounded smartly in August, providing an encouraging indication of the strength of consumer spending. Headline sales were up 1.2% over the month, more than reversing a 0.5% decline in July that now looks to have been caused by seasonality. Spending was broad-based, with all subsectors aside from building materials registering higher sales over August. Looking through the noise in recent reports, the pace of underlying consumer spending looks to be advancing at a healthy rate, in our view. This should help provide some reassurance around the resilience of the U.S. economy in the face of increasing short-term headwinds to growth, including higher interest rates, a renewed spike in oil prices, trade disruptions, and waning support from tax cuts.
All eyes on the Fed –
Talking of higher interest rates, markets overwhelmingly expect the Federal Reserve Open Market Committee (FOMC) to deliver the first increase in U.S. interest rates since 2023 this afternoon. A shift back to policy tightening should reflect a growing concern at the Fed that inflation pressures are proving stickier than anticipated, with the renewed spike in oil prices in recent days likely to add to fears that a return to the central bank's 2% inflation target could be delayed even further. Moreover, with the economy continuing to deliver solid growth, an increasing number of Fed policymakers are likely to judge that interest rates are not restrictive enough at current settings, in our view. Absent any surprises in today's decision, we think the most important aspect of the meeting will be what signals the central bank provides around where policy is heading from here. Chair Warsh has been reluctant to give explicit guidance on the direction for Fed policy, meaning that the market may well instead look to the updated FOMC members' interest rate forecasts for views as to how much tightening the committee sees as appropriate to get inflation back on track.
James McCann

CNBC Reporter & Morning Squawk Writer
Happy Thursday. Breaking news this morning: Nvidia has agreed to buy open-source artificial intelligence platform Hugging Face
for nearly $13 billion.
Stock futures
are mixed this morning after a
winning day
on Wall Street.
Here are five key things investors need to know to start the trading day:
1. Summit up
The G20 wrapped up its two-day Innovation Ministerial yesterday, where technology leaders and government representatives talked artificial intelligence, data centers and tariffs.
Here are some of the biggest headlines out of the gathering:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said that AI will “democratize intelligence” for G20 countries and called the technology “the great equalizer.”
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, meanwhile, said using AI is a “non-negotiable” for countries, comparing the adoption of AI to the adoption of electricity.
Palantir CEO Alex Karp acknowledged that there are “huge dangers” to the technology but pushed back on what he called the “doom message” around AI. He appeared to allude to Anthropic and its CEO, who have warned about the technology’s risks.
On the data center front, Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown said he “really loved” President Donald Trump’s Monday Truth Social post, in which the president said communities who opposed data centers “want to end up being backwards and poor.”
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said that data centers will “bring prosperity” and are “getting a bad rap.” He also downplayed the facilities’ water consumption.
Catch up on all the biggest moments here.
2. Bond, John Bond
After hitting its
highest level since 2023
, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield pulled back in Wednesday’s session, providing relief for other corners of the market.
New York Federal Reserve President John Williams told CNBC yesterday that the recent yield jumps should be seen as
a sign of a strong economy
rather than as market dysfunction. Williams also said he would have to “wait and see” before deciding whether an interest rate hike would be necessary to calm inflation.
The three major averages snapped three-day losing streaks yesterday.
Follow live market updates here.
3. Snow forecast
Snowflake soared 24%
